title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
hook: God shrinks Gideon's army so no one will boast

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon, called mighty while hiding in a winepress. Your line was you, mighty?

Gideon finally has an army, and God's complaint is not that it's too small. In the King James Bible: "The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." Too many. Gideon's men camp by a spring, and below them in the valley lies the camp of Midian, "like grasshoppers for multitude," with camels past counting. Any sensible general would send for more troops. Gideon is told to send people home.

First cut: whoever is fearful and afraid may go home. The text says twenty-two thousand leave and ten thousand stay. Still too many. Second cut: take them down to the water to drink. Some get down on their knees. Some lap, putting their hand to their mouth. Three hundred lap, and those are the ones God keeps: "By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you." The text never says why the lappers. Some preachers say they were the alert ones, keeping their eyes up. Others say the test was arbitrary on purpose, and God simply took the smaller group. Judges gives no reason for the test at all. The reason it does give is back in verse two: so Israel can't say, mine own hand hath saved me. Then the plan, and it's strange. Each of the three hundred gets a trumpet and an empty pitcher with a lamp hidden inside. In the night they spread out around the camp, blow the trumpets, smash the pitchers so the lights blaze out, and cry: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." And then: "they stood every man in his place round about the camp." They don't charge. They hold up their lights and stand still. The camp panics and turns on itself. Notice the order of that cry: the LORD first, Gideon second. The chapter is built so that, afterward, nobody can tell it as a story about their own strength. Less isn't a punishment here. Less is how they find out who did the saving.
screen: `THE TEXT NEVER SAYS WHY THE LAPPERS.`
then, large: `THE SWORD OF THE LORD, AND OF GIDEON.`
`THEY STOOD EVERY MAN IN HIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Name one thing in front of you that you feel under-equipped for: not enough time, money, help or sleep. Instead of listing what you lack, count what you actually have, the way Gideon counted at the water: three hundred is a real number, and so is one free hour, two friends or forty dollars. If you pray, bring the gap to God; if you don't, let the small number be enough for now.
Three hundred. The men who lapped the water: the army God made smaller, so no one could say, my own hand saved me.
Your line: less is enough. Nobody could call it the work of their own hand. Day seven hundred five.

howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of Gideon's three hundred to speak about God's strength showing up in human weakness, and some pair it with Paul's words in Second Corinthians that strength is made perfect in weakness.

chat.says: Why did God shrink Gideon's army instead of sending him more soldiers?
options: So Israel couldn't say, my own hand saved me; less shows who did the saving.
Because God wanted only soldiers who had never fought a battle before.
To save food and water, since the camp couldn't feed thirty-two thousand.
chat.meaning: Verse two gives the reason: lest Israel vaunt themselves, saying, mine own hand hath saved me. Less is how they find out who saved them.

notes: Numbers (twenty-two thousand leave, ten thousand stay, three hundred lap) are taken directly from Judges 7:3, 7:6 and 7:7.
Judges 7:6 says those who lapped put 'their hand to their mouth', while 7:5 compares lapping to a dog; the script follows 7:6. Confirm.

The two popular explanations of the lapping test (the lappers were alert; God took the smaller group) are attributed to 'some preachers' and 'others', and the script says the text gives no reason. Confirm.
